title: Design a News Feed
summary: Posts from everyone you follow, in 200 ms — and the question of when to do the work.

goals.text: Size the read and write load of a feed
Fan-out on read vs fan-out on write
Why celebrities break pure push — and the hybrid fix
What to store, and for whom

steps.title: The brief: a home feed
body: Second design. A social app: people follow each other, and the home screen shows recent posts from everyone you follow, newest first.

What matters: opening the feed must feel instant — under 200 ms. A new post should reach followers within a few seconds, but not necessarily at the same instant for everyone. Eventual consistency is fine: nobody is harmed if a post shows up five seconds late.

callout.text: Notice the freedom in that last requirement. Deciding what does not have to be immediate or exact is what makes large systems possible.

card.title: Requirements
lines: home feed   posts from people I follow
# a new post may take a few seconds

steps.title: Put numbers on it
body: 200 million people use it daily and open the feed about ten times each: 2 billion feed loads a day, or 23,000 a second on average. They write 50 million posts a day — about 600 a second.
So feeds are read roughly 40 times more often than posts are written. And a typical user follows 200 accounts. Remember that number.

callout.text: Two numbers will drive everything that follows: reads outnumber writes 40 to 1, and every feed draws on 200 sources.

card.title: Napkin math
lines: = about 40 feed reads per post written

steps.title: First draft: build the feed when it’s asked for
body: Store posts in a table indexed by (author_id, created_at), sharded by author. To build Alice’s feed: find the 200 accounts she follows, fetch the latest posts of each, merge them by time, return the top 20.
This is the pull model, or fan-out on read. Posting is as cheap as it gets — one insert — and a new post is visible to everyone at once.

callout.text: Nothing is precomputed, so nothing can go stale and nothing needs repairing. For a small app, this is the right design.

changes: + Feed = query 200 authors, merge, keep the top 20

steps.title: The work lands on the wrong side
body: Every feed load fans out to 200 authors spread over many shards, and has to wait for the slowest answer — the fan-out tail from Latency & Throughput.

Worse is the total: 23,000 feed loads a second × 200 lookups = 4.6 million lookups a second, mostly recomputing a result identical to what the same person saw a minute ago. The expensive work sits on the path that runs 40 times more often.

callout.text: When reads far outnumber writes, move the work to write time.

card.title: Cost of pull
lines: # and each load waits for the slowest shard

steps.title: Flip it: deliver posts when they’re written
body: Give every user a ready-made feed: a list in a cache, newest first. When Ana posts, a fan-out worker looks up her followers and adds the post to each of their lists. This is the push model, or fan-out on write.
Opening the feed is now one read of one list. The fan-out runs behind a queue (Message Queues), so Ana’s post returns immediately and her followers see it a second or two later.

callout.text: The arithmetic works: 600 posts/s × 200 followers ≈ 120,000 small cache writes a second — far cheaper than 4.6 million lookups.

changes: + Feed cache: one list per user

steps.title: Store ids, not posts
body: Each feed list holds only post ids — a few bytes apiece — and only the newest 800 or so. When a feed is read, the API fetches the posts themselves in one batch from the post store (“hydration”).
Keeping a single copy of every post means an edit or a delete happens in one place. A deleted post is simply dropped during hydration; nobody has to chase it through millions of lists.

callout.text: 200 million lists × 800 ids × 8 bytes ≈ 1.3 TB of memory: a big cache cluster, but an ordinary one. Storing whole posts would cost a hundred times as much.

changes: ~ Feed lists hold post ids only, capped at 800
+ Posts fetched in one batch at read time
~ Edits and deletes happen in one place

steps.title: Case: fifty million followers
body: A pop star with 50 million followers posts. That single post becomes 50 million cache writes. Even at 100,000 writes a second, delivery takes more than eight minutes — and the queue is so backed up that everyone else’s posts wait behind it.
It’s the hot-key problem from Sharding: one unusually heavy key overwhelms a design tuned for the average.

callout.text: Averages hide this. The typical account has 200 followers; a few thousand accounts have millions — and they post at the busiest moments.

changes: + A celebrity posts to 50 M followers
− 50 M feed writes for one post

steps.title: Hybrid: push for most, pull for the famous
body: Treat the two kinds of account differently. Ordinary users keep fan-out on write. Accounts above a threshold — say 100,000 followers — are not fanned out at all.

When Alice opens her feed, the API reads her ready-made list and pulls the latest posts of the handful of celebrities she follows — each one a single cached timeline — then merges the two. A few extra lookups per read, instead of 50 million writes per post.

callout.text: Neither pure strategy survives real data. Large designs usually end up as a hybrid, split along exactly the dimension that is skewed.

changes: ~ Accounts over 100 k followers: no fan-out
+ Their posts are merged in at read time

steps.title: Case: feeds nobody reads
body: Of everyone who follows Ana, perhaps a third opened the app this month. Fanning out to the rest fills memory with lists nobody will ever look at.

So skip them: fan out only to followers active in the last 30 days, and let everyone else’s list expire. When a lapsed user comes back, build their feed once with the pull model, cache it, and resume pushing.

callout.text: The pull path never goes away. It is how feeds are created, repaired and rebuilt — push is an optimisation layered on top of it.

changes: ~ Fan out only to recently active followers
+ Returning users: rebuilt by pull, once

steps.title: Scrolling: cursors, not page numbers
body: Alice scrolls down for more. “Page 2” would mean “skip 20, take 20” — but three new posts have arrived at the top since page 1, so she’d see three posts twice.
Use a cursor instead (see REST, RPC & GraphQL): “give me 20 posts older than post 9017”. The position is tied to a post, not to a count, so new arrivals can’t shift it.

callout.text: Time-ordered ids (Unique IDs at Scale) make this easy: “older than” is simply “id less than”.

card.title: Cursor pagination
lines: = stays put while new posts arrive

steps.title: Case: the feed cache is wiped
body: A bad deploy flushes the feed cache. Every feed is gone — and nothing of value is lost. Posts and the follow graph are the source of truth; feed lists are derived data that can be rebuilt from them.

The danger is a stampede: millions of users rebuilding by pull at the same moment. So rebuild lazily, only when a user actually opens the app; cap how many rebuilds run at once; and serve a thinner feed until the cache is warm again.

callout.text: Know which of your data is the truth and which is a convenience. You can afford to be relaxed about the second only because you are strict about the first.

changes: ~ Feeds rebuilt on demand from posts + follows
~ Rebuilds throttled to protect the post store

A ranked feed adds one more stage — score the candidates before returning them — but the plumbing underneath is the same.
